asking.answers: Each question comes with two to four suggested answers, plus “Something else” and “Just draw it”.
asking.brief: Once there’s enough detail, the clarifier writes a short brief, usually one or two sentences, and selects a style: photography, illustration, minimal or 3D render.
asking.cap: The three-question limit is enforced in code. I don’t rely on the model to stop itself. If it tries to ask a fourth question, I ignore the question and draw with the information already available.
asking.enough: Before drawing, a clarifier model checks whether the description has enough detail.
asking.needs: I look for three things: a subject, a style, and at least one of setting, lighting or framing. If something is missing, the agent asks about one thing at a time, in that order.
asking.pipeline: The drawing pipeline works from that brief, not the full conversation.
asking.title: Asking before drawing

drawing.cache: That gives identical images the same URL, so the browser can cache them for a year.
drawing.first_reviewer: The first version of the reviewer had a serious problem: it failed on every image, and the fallback code saved each failure as a pass with made-up scores.
drawing.into_code: So I moved the sequence into code:
drawing.no_reviewer: That was worse than having no review at all. Now, if no reviewer is available, I still return the picture, but without a score and with a note explaining that it wasn’t checked.
drawing.once: The prompt is written once per picture, with one additional attempt if the review fails.
drawing.order: My first version was written in Python and let the model choose which tool to call next. But the prompt already specified the order, and tool calling didn’t fit well with a pipeline where each step could switch providers.
drawing.pass: A picture passes if its overall score is at least 7 and its relevance score is at least 6. If the first attempt fails, the reviewer can send up to three notes back to the prompt writer for one more attempt. I keep whichever of the two pictures is better.
drawing.positive: I keep the prompt focused on what I want to see. Telling an image model what not to include can end up putting those very things into the picture.
drawing.prompt: The prompt writer turns the brief into 60–120 words describing what should appear in the picture.
drawing.review: A vision model checks the generated picture for relevance, quality, style and composition. Each category gets a score out of 10, along with an overall score and suggestions.
drawing.step_again: Generate one more picture and keep the better result.
drawing.step_rewrite: If it fails review, send the reviewer’s notes back to the prompt writer.
drawing.step_write: Write an image prompt from the brief.
drawing.storage: Pictures go into a storage bucket, with the filename derived from the contents of the image.
drawing.title: Drawing

failover.alike: Running out of quota and running out of credit look similar, but they need different handling.
failover.before_split: I originally treated both cases as exhausted quota. That meant an empty account was retried every 30 minutes, even though nothing had changed.
failover.chain_pictures: **Images:** OpenAI `gpt-image-1`, Cloudflare Flux Schnell, Pollinations Flux, then Gemini Image.
failover.chain_text: **Text:** `gpt-4o-mini`, Llama 3.3 70B on Groq, then Gemini Flash models.
failover.chains_intro: I use separate fallback chains for image generation, text and image review.
failover.everything: If every provider fails, the error tells the person whether trying again later is likely to help.
failover.first_version: The first version always told people to try again shortly, even when waiting wouldn’t fix anything.
failover.groq: Groq isn’t part of the review chain because none of the models available to my account can accept an image.
failover.quota: When a provider runs out of quota, I skip it for 30 minutes, or longer if the provider asks for it. When the account runs out of credit, I skip it for a day because retrying won’t help until someone tops up the account.
failover.refill: If at least one provider has a quota that will refill, I suggest trying later. If none of them can recover without more credit or some other intervention, I say so.
failover.retries: Other errors get two retries, one second apart and then two seconds apart.
failover.timeouts: If a call times out, I move straight to the next provider. A provider that has already hung once isn’t worth waiting on again during the same request.
failover.timeouts_intro: Each type of model call has its own timeout:
failover.title: When a provider stops answering

governing.check_classifier: **Classifier.** Decide whether the message is actually asking for a picture.
governing.check_limits: **Limits.** Reject requests that exceed the allowance before saving anything.
governing.check_moderation: **Moderation.** Use OpenAI’s moderation model to check for unsafe content.
governing.check_rules: **Rules.** Catch obvious problems in code, without calling a model.
governing.checks: Every message passes through four checks, from cheapest to most expensive:
governing.clarifier: Only messages that pass all four reach the clarifier, which decides whether there’s enough detail to draw.
governing.classifier: That’s what the classifier is for.
governing.earlier_turns: The earlier turns matter. A reply like “illustration, at dusk” doesn’t mean much on its own, but it makes sense in the context of the conversation.
governing.failed_check: If moderation succeeds but the classifier fails, the message can continue because the safety check has already passed. If neither check runs, the turn fails without drawing anything. I don’t want unchecked text reaching the image model.
governing.failed_intro: I don’t treat every model error the same way.
governing.left_off: I deliberately left words like “naked” and “murder” off the list. A naked mole rat and a murder of crows are perfectly reasonable subjects for a picture. Moderation is better suited to judging those words in context.
governing.markers: It receives the new message alongside earlier turns, marked with `<<<MESSAGE>>>`{secondary} and `<<<END>>>`{secondary}. Its prompt tells it to treat the marked text as data to classify, not as instructions to follow.
governing.moderation: Moderation is free and useful for safety checks, but it doesn’t tell me whether a message is asking for a picture. “Hello”, “test” and a question about the weather aren’t image requests, even if they’re harmless.
governing.outcomes: A limit rejection returns an error and isn’t recorded. A refusal from the rules, moderation or classifier is handled differently: the message is withdrawn from the conversation, but still counts towards the person’s allowance.
governing.questions: The clarifier can ask up to three questions before drawing with the information it has.
governing.refusals: The image providers have their own safety filters, too. If a provider refuses a prompt that passed my checks, I return a refusal rather than trying the same prompt with another provider.
governing.rules: The rules catch a short list of unambiguous words, prompt injection phrases such as “ignore previous instructions” and “developer mode”, links the agent can’t open, messages shorter than three letters, and long strings with very little character variety.
governing.rules_intro: Some requests don’t need a model to spot.
governing.title: What gets through
governing.title_failed_check: When a check fails to run

how_it_works.describe: Describe the picture you want and its setting.
how_it_works.follow_up: If something important is missing, the agent asks a question. You can pick a suggested answer or type your own.
how_it_works.limits: Requests for violent or explicit images are refused. You can have one conversation running at a time.
how_it_works.title: How it works

limits.checked: The `ImageAgentSend`{info} mutation checks these limits on every request. `ImageAgentAllowance`{info} reports how many pictures remain, the limit, when the next message is allowed, whether a turn is running, and which conversations are active.
limits.cost: Pictures cost money to generate, and the agent doesn’t require an account. I needed limits at both the individual and service level.
limits.counts: Usage counts live in MongoDB rather than in memory, so restarting the server doesn’t reset anyone’s limits. A picture counts as soon as drawing starts, even if a provider later refuses the request or generation fails.
limits.day: A day means the last 24 hours, not the calendar day.
limits.network: I don’t read or store network addresses, so people sharing the same network don’t share an allowance.
limits.person_turn: One turn running at a time
limits.refused: A request rejected by the limits returns `TOO_MANY_REQUESTS`{error} without being recorded. That also prevents a double-click from consuming allowance or repeatedly resetting the cooldown.
limits.session: A person is identified by their session.
limits.shared: When a daily or hourly limit is reached, the error doesn’t reveal which limit was hit or when it resets. That makes it harder to use the error response to work out how to get around the limits.
limits.title: Limits
limits.token: On the first visit, they pass a Turnstile check and receive a token. Every subsequent request is counted against that session. Clearing cookies or switching devices creates a new session with a fresh allowance. I’m fine with that trade-off.
limits.turnstile: Turnstile makes it harder to automate repeated visits and bypass the limits.

retrieval.assumed: I initially assumed I’d need embeddings and a vector database. I didn’t.
retrieval.brief: The clarifier can also update the saved brief and style. If someone asks for a change after seeing a picture, it reads the existing brief alongside the conversation and writes a new one. The prompt writer and reviewer only see the brief and style, so they don’t need the entire conversation.
retrieval.cheap: This ran on every keystroke, so it had to be cheap. Counting shared words took one database read.
retrieval.moved: I moved the search to the browser, where it filters the conversations already loaded on the start page. The API lookup is no longer needed.
retrieval.plain_text: The classifier and clarifier read the conversation as plain text, with one line per turn labelled `Person:` or `Agent:`. Progress updates, pictures and refused messages are left out.
retrieval.rewind: Asking an earlier message again restores the brief and style from that point in the conversation.
retrieval.similar: An earlier version showed similar past conversations while someone was typing. It split the input into words, dropped short and common words, then compared the remaining words against the person’s 50 most recent conversations. It returned up to three matches if at least 60% of the words matched.
retrieval.source: Everything the models need comes from the conversation they’re working on, along with the brief and style saved on that conversation.
retrieval.title: Retrieval, without a vector store
retrieval.vector_store: I’d consider a vector store if I needed to search beyond a person’s current conversations, for example to find briefs from other people’s pictures that scored well. For a handful of conversations per person, matching words was enough.

sending.broker: With two servers, it breaks: a turn running on one server can’t send updates to a browser connected to the other. I’d need a shared message broker, such as Redis, before running multiple instances.
sending.handle: I handle this when a conversation is read or a new message is sent. If a turn has been quiet for too long, I mark it as failed and let the person continue.
sending.idle: When the turn finishes, the conversation returns to `IDLE`{confirm}.
sending.marks_failed: The conversation gets the message: “I stopped before I could finish the last request.”
sending.mutation: When you send a message, the `ImageAgentSend`{info} mutation checks your limits, saves the message, starts the agent and returns the current conversation.
sending.not_at_startup: I don’t do this at startup. With several servers, one that has just started can’t tell a dead turn from one another server is still running.
sending.one_turn: A conversation can only have one turn running at a time.
sending.pub_sub: Updates use an in-memory pub/sub system inside the Node process. That works fine with one server.
sending.restart: A deployment can kill a running turn and leave its conversation stuck in `THINKING`{warning} or `DRAWING`{info}. Since only one turn can run at a time, the person can’t continue until that state is cleared.
sending.same_write: When a message arrives, I save it and mark the conversation as `THINKING`{warning} in the same database write. That way, two requests can’t both start a turn against the same conversation. If it’s already `THINKING`{warning} or `DRAWING`{info}, another request is rejected.
sending.streams: While the agent works, it sends short status updates so people know what’s happening, whether it’s checking a request, working on the prompt or drawing.
sending.subscription: Drawing takes about a minute, so I didn’t want to keep the original request open while it runs. The browser gets the rest of the updates through a GraphQL subscription, `ImageAgentThreadUpdated`{info}. Whenever something changes, the server sends the conversation back to the browser.
sending.title: Sending a message

what_this_is.code: Calling the models was the easy part. Most of the work went into everything around them: limits, error handling, retries and fallbacks. Several of those came from things the first version got wrong.
what_this_is.summary: You describe a picture, and the agent draws it. If your description leaves something important out, it asks a follow-up question. After three questions, it draws with whatever information it has. A second model checks the result before you see it.
what_this_is.why: I built this to figure out what it takes to put an AI feature in front of real people without letting costs get out of hand or unsafe requests slip through.

allowance.description: Per person: one turn running at a time, five seconds between messages, 40 messages and five pictures a day. Across everyone: 1,000 messages and 200 pictures a day, and 10 new people an hour. Both sets are checked when ImageAgentSend runs, which takes a thread id and the text. The ImageAgentAllowance query reports the person’s remaining pictures, the limit, when the next message is allowed, whether a turn is busy, and the running conversations.
allowance.row_turn: One turn running at a time
allowance.title: Limits and the schema

context.description: The conversation, as Person and Agent lines with refused messages removed, goes to the classifier and the clarifier. The clarifier also reads and updates the brief and style saved on the thread. The prompt writer and the reviewer read only the brief and style. The prompt writer’s prompt goes to the image model, the picture goes to the reviewer, and a failed review sends its notes back to the prompt writer once.
context.title: What each model reads

drawing.description: From the brief, a prompt is written, the picture drawn and reviewed. A pass saves the best attempt. A failed review sends up to three notes back to the prompt writer for one more attempt. Every call goes through a chain of providers; for pictures that is gpt-image-1, Flux Schnell on Cloudflare, Flux on Pollinations, then Gemini. Each provider times out and moves on, gives other errors two more tries, and is skipped for 30 minutes when its quota is spent or a day when it is out of credit.
drawing.legend_bottom: the order providers are tried in for Draw
drawing.legend_top: once per picture, one retry after a failed review
drawing.line_provider_error: other error: 2 more tries, 1 s then 2 s apart
drawing.line_provider_quota: quota spent: skip 30 min · out of credit: skip a day
drawing.line_provider_timeout: timeout: move on (30 s text, 45 s review, 90 s image)
drawing.title: Drawing, and failover

governing.description: A message passes limits, rules, moderation and a classifier in that order before the clarifier reads it. A limit refuses with an error that is not recorded. Rules, moderation and the classifier refuse with a refusal message, and the person’s message is withdrawn but still counted. The clarifier either asks a question, up to three per picture, or starts drawing.
governing.legend_green: moves the message to the next check
governing.title: $t(article.governing.title)

how_it_works.description: A message is sent with ImageAgentSend and checked against the limits. It is either refused with TOO_MANY_REQUESTS and not recorded, or saved and counted, after which ImageAgentAllowance shows what is left.
how_it_works.title: What happens when you send

overview.description: The browser sends messages to the API over a GraphQL mutation and gets updates back over a subscription. The API keeps conversations, jobs and assets in MongoDB, calls a moderation endpoint and three provider chains for text, vision and images, and uploads pictures to a storage bucket that the browser reads through the site’s assets route.
overview.legend_dashed: updates and assets come back from the server
overview.title: How the pieces connect

turn.description: Sequence of one turn. The browser sends the message; the API checks limits and stale turns, saves it and sets the conversation to THINKING, and returns at once. The turn then runs on: checks and the clarifier call the models, each step is saved and pushed to the browser over the subscription, the picture is drawn and reviewed, and the conversation goes back to IDLE with the picture.
turn.title: From send to picture

error_empty: Say what the picture should show.
error_limited: Too many requests for now. Try again later.
error_too_long: Keep it to {{max}} characters or fewer.
error_unreachable: Could not reach the conversation. Check your connection and reload.
